items.title: [phys.org] Full-scale wave test shows salt marshes can buffer coastal storms
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Researchers moved 306 square meters of intact salt marsh into the Delta Flume, a large wave-testing facility in Delft, Netherlands, and exposed it to waves as high as 2 meters. After 21 hours, the marsh surface had eroded by an average of just 7 millimeters, while its vegetation suffered progressive damage. The study found that plants can reduce wave energy by more than 10%, and by as much as 50% on lower-energy coasts with waves up to 1 meter. Their effect declines as waves grow higher and vegetation is lost. Researchers say marshes could work alongside dikes and seawalls, not replace them. A Spanish coastal-engineering expert questioned how well the Dutch experiment applies to other coastlines, citing wave periods and mobile seabeds among other factors.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN urges steep fossil-fuel cuts as 1.5°C overshoot becomes unavoidable
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The United Nations Environment Programme’s (UNEP) 2026 Emissions Gap Report says governments must now limit the scale and duration of global warming beyond 1.5°C, rather than try to prevent that threshold from being crossed. Its lowest-overshoot pathway would cap warming at 1.7°C to 1.8°C around mid-century, with about a 50% chance of returning to 1.5°C by 2100. Following that pathway requires greenhouse-gas emissions to fall 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, compared with 2025. The report says existing national climate pledges would cut emissions by only 5% to 8% by 2030 and 11% to 15% by 2035. If current policies continue, warming could reach 2.8°C this century; full delivery of pledges would still leave it at about 2.6°C. The pathway also calls for sharply reducing coal-fired electricity generation and scaling up carbon removal. The report warns that the required reductions are far beyond current plans. Governments are due to discuss climate action at the COP31 summit, scheduled to open in Antalya on Nov. 9.

items.title: [theglobeandmail.com] Smith tells UCP separatists to accept referendum result or leave the party
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Wednesday told separatists to stop publicly advocating for independence or leave her United Conservative Party (UCP), after voters rejected moving toward a binding separation referendum by roughly three to one. The nonbinding Oct. 19 referendum also asked about immigration and constitutional changes. Preliminary results showed majorities for eight of the other nine proposals. Smith said people may hold their own views, but UCP candidates, provincial board members and constituency association representatives must support “a strong Alberta within a united Canada.” She warned that a year of internal division could cost the party the provincial election, scheduled for October 2027. Separatist organizers say they will seek influence inside the party rather than form a new one. They are organizing for the UCP’s annual meeting, which opens Nov. 27, where delegates elect board members and set party policy. Smith has not detailed how she will enforce the new rules.

items.title: [downes.ca] Principles and Practice of Deep Representation Learning
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Sam Buchanan, Druv Pai, Peng Wang, Yi Ma, GitHub, Oct 22, 2026

This is "a modern fully open-source textbook exploring why and how deep neural networks learn compact and information-dense representations of high-dimensional real-world data." It's a daunting read - and to be honest, I gave the first chapter a careful read but have only skimmed the rest (though it's now on my virtual bookshelf for future reference). I think people who are serious about understanding how we learn and how machines emulate this should at the very least read that first chapter. It contains what is to my understanding an accurate history of artificial intelligence (including the important early work in computation, cybernetics, and information theory). The aim of the book is to give us a framework that explains how neural networks work to generate intelligence. They authors write, "intelligence is not about collecting all informative data in advance and training a model to memorize their (low-dimensional) distribution. Instead, it requires computational mechanisms that can continuously improve current knowledge of the distribution and acquire new information when needed. A fundamental characteristic of any intelligent being or system - whether an animal, a human, a civilization, or the entire scientific community - is the ability to continuously improve or gain new information or knowledge on its own."

items.title: [thehackernews.com] Attackers compromise AI gateway LiteLLM 1.107.0 to steal credentials
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Attackers released a malicious version of LiteLLM, an open-source gateway for connecting to AI models, distributing version 1.107.0 through the Python Package Index (PyPI) and Docker images on Oct. 21. The package installed a credential stealer and a backdoor that could collect cloud and AI service keys, private keys, browser data and other secrets. The code could run whenever Python started, even in programs that did not use LiteLLM. LiteLLM said attackers used three engineers’ GitHub credentials to alter and approve the release, but it has not identified how they obtained those credentials. PyPI removed the package, and affected Docker image tags were removed or replaced. The company advised users to rebuild from a clean environment, rotate exposed credentials and use version 1.106.2 while the investigation continues.

Scale and warning: LiteLLM receives about 23 million weekly downloads. Security researchers urged teams to investigate any host or continuous integration (CI) runner where Python ran after installation (theregister.com).

items.title: [scitechdaily.com] Stanford team revives bleached corals through brief clone contact
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Stanford researchers report that bleached coral fragments fully recovered within seven weeks in laboratory tests after brief contact with healthy, genetically identical clones, according to a study published Oct. 14 in *Science Advances*. Contact lasting five days to a week was sometimes enough; bleached fragments kept a few millimeters away from healthy partners died. Microscopic channels in the corals’ tissues aligned, allowing beneficial algae to move between fragments within three days. Inside bleached fragments, algae populations doubled every four days during the second week. The method requires matching clones, limiting its use across reefs. The researchers plan to test other ways to deliver algae, including collecting it from healthy corals before heat waves.

items.title: [library.hbs.edu] AI agents spread as job, safety and investment risks draw scrutiny
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Companies and governments are adopting AI agents that can carry out tasks, while researchers and policymakers examine their effects on jobs, security and investment. Google CEO Sundar Pichai said he uses agents to summarize internal discussions and track computing use, but humans still make consequential decisions about allocating resources. Google has also introduced agentic AI for public agencies, and the United Arab Emirates plans to shift half of federal government operations and services to autonomous agents within two years. Stanford University researchers report that employment in AI-exposed software development and customer-service jobs fell by more than 4% this year, while Harvard researchers say current labor-market signals offer little certainty about AI’s longer-term effects. Central bankers are assessing potential effects on wages and productivity, and a University of Hawaiʻi analysis estimates that AI investment and related stock gains have supported U.S. growth and consumer spending. Security teams report difficulty verifying agents’ answers, and AI infrastructure borrowers, including CoreWeave, face rising credit risks. Center for Internet Security senior director of threat intelligence TJ Sayers said autonomous AI attacks are no longer hypothetical. Agent use remained in single digits across almost every business function, according to the Stanford 2026 AI Index cited by The National.

items.title: [Fast Company] Healthcare has a churn problem
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

I was diagnosed with anorexia at 10 years old. Over the next several years, my family and I navigated a healthcare system that was mostly focused on how many days I stayed in a hospital bed instead of whether I was getting better.

I spent my entire freshman year of high school in and out of facilities, counting down 45-minute therapy slots while fighting a brain disorder that forces you to battle your own mind upwards of six times a day. The bills came in, claims were processed, and the checkboxes were ticked, but I was still struggling with anorexia.

Decades later, now as a founder and CEO of an eating disorder treatment program, I realize my teenage experience embodied the traditional healthcare business model to a T.

THE ONLY INDUSTRY WHERE PRODUCT FAILURE IS PROFITABLE

In traditional healthcare, revenue is tied to volume: More time in session results in more revenue. The more appointments booked, the more the facility can bill; the longer someone stays in treatment—and the more times they relapse—the more profitable the facility becomes.

If any consumer tech or hardware startup ran on this model, it would fail fast. It’s like going to an auto repair shop that charges by the hour, sends you home with a car that still stalls, and then charges you again when you have to tow it back into the shop.

The main problem is industry alignment. Fee-for-service models reward visit volume and usually lead to fragmented, episodic care. Value-based outcome models, on the other hand, tie reimbursement directly to clinical and financial outcomes. If we want a healthcare system that can keep up with rising costs and demand, we need to align incentives around real, measurable outcomes.

BUILD WHAT WORKS

Tying financial compensation to real-world outcomes gives leaders the flexibility to build better products that result in positive outcomes for all parties involved. In healthcare, that means patients, their families, providers, and health insurance plans.

For example, when we started Equip, we knew that once-a-week therapy wasn’t enough to address a complex eating disorder, but the traditional fee-for-service billing system made it nearly impossible to bill for anything else. By partnering with forward-thinking health insurance plans to develop value-based payment structures, we designed the treatment model families needed: a team of doctors, dietitians, therapists, and coaches delivered virtually. This approach provides the right dose of care when patients need it, without uprooting their daily routines or stopping them from building a life worth living.

WHAT DOES “GOOD” LOOK LIKE?

The catch, however, is that the healthcare industry has historically lacked a consensus on what “good” means. Defining quality is particularly difficult in eating disorders, where recovery isn’t as simple as a blood test or a healed bone. The field uses two tools—the EDE-Q and the PARDI-AR—to set severity thresholds, but neither gets into what “getting better” means. It also requires a long-term view, which can clash with an industry where most health insurance plans operate on 12- to 24-month budget cycles.

When I was 10, that meant staying in a hospital bed long enough for my vitals to stabilize. But as I found out through many cycles of treatment, that didn’t lead to me getting better.

To solve the national mental health crisis, we need an economic framework where doing good and doing good business are the same. By replacing the traditional model with outcome-based partnerships, we aren’t just building more efficient companies, but delivering on healthcare’s biggest promise: building a product that works.

Kristina Saffran is cofounder and CEO of Equip.
